A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same template-memorization reconstruction attack despite the changed title. Their complete text, figures, tables, and Appendix A support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v3 reports original image-generation experiments, a 70-participant user study, real-world prompt tests, controlled synthetic experiments, and reconstructed examples in Appendix A.

after.justification: v4 retains these original results and adds similarity-metric analysis in Figure 12 and BE-PRSS detection and mitigation experiments in Section 4.9.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains collocation-plus-descriptor prompts, pretrained segmentation, fixed-region CLIP similarity above 0.95, cliques of at least two images, and manual inspection/source tracing. Evaluating BE-PRSS does not modify the proposed attack.

E1.justification: Appendix A adds the Bag/Backpack product category, and Section 4.9 introduces a mitigated-generation test scenario. The principal datasets, attacked models, user-study coverage, and synthetic coffee-mug, tea-cup, and T-shirt scenarios remain.

E2.justification: v4 substantially expands evaluated comparisons through BE-PRSS detection and mitigation in Section 4.9 and SSCD, CLIP, and L2 comparisons with human judgments in Figure 12. Earlier attack comparisons remain; the new Table 1 summarizes prior-work counts rather than establishing matched reruns.

E3.justification: Section 4 revises the reported tested-collocation count from 112 to 108, without establishing a rerun. Added protocols include ROC/AUC evaluation and operating thresholds, plus BE-PRSS threshold 1.0 and mitigation testing on 43 collocations using 25 ChatGPT prompt variations and an any-seed success criterion. Existing study designs remain.

E4.justification: Two substantive analyses are added: Figure 12 tests automatic similarity measures against the user-study evidence, and Section 4.9 examines detection failures, reconstruction persistence under mitigation, and utility degradation. The earlier interpolation, perturbation, leakage, synthetic, and SD 3.5 analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The new BE-PRSS experiments specify three generation seeds per prompt. This does not establish increased repetitions of existing experiments. Figure 4 retains its five-permutation mean and 95% confidence interval, and Figure 11 retains cross-participant confidence intervals.

E6.justification: The summary changes from 63 templates across 112 collocations to 67 across 108, newly reporting 43 successful collocations. Figure 12 adds AUCs of 0.810 for human judgments, 0.806 for SSCD, 0.608 for CLIP, and 0.760 for L2. Section 4.9 adds detection accuracy/precision/recall of 0.595/0.520/0.722 and mitigation results of 28 versus 22 successful collocations out of 43, with utility degradation. Appendix examples also change. These are revised and additional results, not a demonstrated same-setting performance gain.

T1.justification: Neither version contains substantive formal proofs or theoretical derivations. The existing mathematical content and template-group concepts remain; added similarity-score notation and ROC reporting do not introduce new formal theory.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the claims of low-resource reconstruction with little or no training-set access, natural prompts reproducing memorized elements and people, and an e-commerce-template vulnerability. The new title and supporting evaluations do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4.9 attributes limited mitigation effectiveness to prompt variations failing to address many-to-many keyword/template associations. The new Discussion explains localized and multisource copying and explicitly acknowledges attribution and manual-inspection scalability limits. Section 4.4 also adds a qualification about upward similarity bias from shared prompts.

D1.justification: v4 removes the explicit public-code URL from the abstract while retaining Appendix A's repository mention without an address; this removes access information but does not establish that the repository became unavailable. Section 4.9 adds script and prompt-variation instructions. Existing hardware, checkpoints, and attack implementation details remain.

R1.justification: v4 adds Chen et al.'s bright-ending-attention work and positions the attack against its BE-PRSS detection and mitigation methods. Other cited works remain identifiable despite bibliography reordering and metadata revisions; Table 1 consolidates comparisons with already-discussed attacks.

P1.justification: The title and abstract are revised, scattered wording and reference placeholders are edited, and Section 4.9, Discussion, and Impact Statement are added. Most existing prose and the section sequence remain intact; the bibliography is also restyled and reordered.

P2.justification: v4 adds Table 1 and the ROC plot in Figure 12, changes Figure 4 from text-wrapped to centered placement, and reflows retained figures. Appendix A adds and revises image grids and separates Comforter and Duvet Cover displays. Most existing illustrations retain their content.

improvement.justification: Compared with v3, Figure 12 provides quantitative evidence about similarity metrics and their operating thresholds, while Section 4.9 directly tests an existing detector and mitigation method. The new Discussion also makes attribution and scalability limitations clearer. These strengthen the existing study, with a limited reproducibility drawback from removing the explicit code-repository link.
